name: Persimmon
lede: Persimmon is the reddish orange of the ripe persimmon fruit, and a color name that books also stretch to the red-brown of the tree's wood.

sections.title: The fruit and the wood
sections.body:
Paterson's dictionary defines persimmon as a reddish orange, the color of the fruit of that name [1]. The same entry adds a second sense, the red-brown of persimmon wood [1].

The name is easy to confuse with another fruit word. Pastoureau notes that *khaki* does not come from the French name of the exotic persimmon fruit, *kaki*; it comes from a Hindustani word meaning earth or dust color [2]. The two words only sound alike. For the dull military shade, see [[khaki]].

sections.title: The juice that waterproofs
sections.body:
Persimmon is also a material. In China and Japan, stencils for resist-dyed indigo cloth were cut from mulberry paper made waterproof with tung oil or persimmon juice [3]. Balfour-Paul adds that persimmon juice, with its natural tannin, was one ingredient of the pastes used in resists on indigo-dyed cloth, alongside bean starch, red peppers and egg white [4].

So the fruit appears in the story of blue before it appears in the story of orange. The juice protected the stencil that kept the dye off the cloth [3][4].

sections.title: In painting
sections.body: St Clair observes that artists have relied on reds from oxblood up to persimmon for drama and depth, and she links the Pre-Raphaelites to such reds [5]. Persimmon sits near [[orange]], [[orange-red]] and [[khaki]] in the name graph.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
Our name graph first records persimmon in a RAL list of 1927, then in Maerz and Paul in 1930 and ISCC-NBS in 1955 [6]. That is a date for the standard, not for the word.

In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within the match threshold of persimmon appears in 25 paintings, 0.11 per cent, and in 29 by the within-painting measure [7]. It is rarer than 57 per cent of the named colors [7]. It peaks in the 1700s, in 10 of 3,449 paintings, 0.3 per cent, or 1.9 times what those museums' holdings would predict [7]. In every one of the 29 paintings it plays an accent, as a small lit patch [7]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a color match is not a pigment test [7].
